content.p: The Chicanos Motorcycle Club is a small but widely reported name in the European biker scene. Police and journalists in Germany, Sweden and Norway have described it as a supporter club of the Bandidos, the outlaw club that has long fought the Hells Angels for territory. The records that survive in the press are mostly reports of arrests, trials and bans rather than any history written by the club itself, and they show a group that drew police attention in several places: a Berlin street fight in 2007, an extortion investigation in 2008, a ban on one German chapter in 2009, a trial in western Sweden in 2013 and a nationwide ban on its badge in 2017.

The articles quoted here describe individuals who were suspected, charged or convicted, and they should be read that way. Where a report relies on police statements, the account below says so. Nothing here shows that every member of the club, or the club as a whole, was involved in the crimes described.
content.h2: What a support club is for
content.p: The Chicanos belong to a family of clubs that sit beneath the big names of the biker world. In 2013 a senior Swedish detective, Örjan Magnusson of the police surveillance unit for eastern Fyrbodal, described the Chicanos' local branch as a sub-unit of the Bandidos and compared it to the older group X-Team: the same model under a different name. A Swedish police press officer, Jörgen Nygren, told the Göteborgs-Tidningen that the group was only six or seven people in all.

Berlin police used the word "Supporterclub" in 2008 for the Chicanos MC El Centro, in a release that also named the Bandidos MC Centro. In 2010 the Berliner Zeitung introduced the Chicanos as a supporter club of the Bandidos, and in 2015 Arbetarbladet in Sweden called the Chicanos in Sandviken a supporter group of the larger and better-known Bandidos.

Police in Norway offered a theory of why such clubs spread. In 2014 the national police intelligence unit Kripos said Bandidos had been setting up Chicanos support clubs in several places in Norway, which it assumed to be an answer to the Hells Angels' creation of Devils Choice MC there the year before. Kripos added that it was too early to say whether this would change the balance between the so-called one-percent clubs. A trend report published in 2015 said that the number of supporter clubs and support groups was one reason the one-percent scene in Norway was larger and more fragmented than ever, and that more supporter clubs meant more recruitment.

An early reported clash involving the Chicanos took place in Reinickendorf, in north Berlin. According to the Berliner Morgenpost and Welt, members of the Bandidos and the Chicanos had a fight with members of an Arab extended family already known to the police, in front of the bikers' clubhouse on Residenzstraße on a Monday evening at about 7 p.m. Both papers called it the first time the bikers had clashed with members of that family. The reason for the quarrel was not known. It began as an argument, the Morgenpost reported, and escalated into a fight with knives, machetes and baseball bats.

One biker and two Arab men, aged 26 and 30, were hurt, one of them seriously. The Morgenpost reported that one of the injured men left hospital after outpatient treatment for a stab wound to the upper body, while the other was in surgery until the next morning but was no longer in danger of dying. The bikers outnumbered their opponents and drove them off. Police found most of those involved gone when they arrived, but arrested four bikers. The special deployment unit (SEK) searched the home in Neukölln of the less seriously injured man, because police could not rule out that he was armed.

The affair then became a quarrel inside the justice system. Police officers, quoted without being named, criticised the duty judge, who had refused a search warrant for the clubhouse on the night of the fight and issued one only the next day, after 1 p.m. The officers said this delayed the investigation by 18 hours and left six riot police standing outside the building in the meantime. A justice spokeswoman told the papers that the warrant could not be issued earlier because the owner of the premises was not known. The Morgenpost added a claim of its own, from its own inquiries: that several Bandidos had gathered and planned an attack on the Arabs but dropped it, fearing the family would have brought reinforcements.

Investigators were quoted as seeing two possible motives, injured honour or a struggle for power in the criminal world, and as expecting retaliation. One officer said the family members would not let such an incident rest, and that further clashes in coming weeks might leave people seriously injured or dead. He also noted that the Bandidos had spent recent months in territorial fights with the Hells Angels.

A year later the same clubhouse address was in a police press release. Berlin police and prosecutors announced in early August 2008 that about 150 officers from the state criminal police and two riot-police units had carried out warrants against members of motorcycle clubs in Charlottenburg and Reinickendorf. Four men were suspects: two aged 23 and 32 from the Bandidos MC Centro, and two aged 24 and 25 from the supporter club Chicanos MC El Centro. Police said the four were suspected of trying to extort a five-figure sum from a 27-year-old business owner in a venue near Luisenplatz in Charlottenburg, and that the inquiry had begun the previous Sunday evening.

A judge issued arrest warrants for all four and nine search warrants, including for the two clubhouses on Residenzstraße. Police said the businessman met the 32-year-old suspect and a 33-year-old Bandidos member at the venue again the next evening and that handcuffs went on the two of them at 19:18, that the 23- and 24-year-old suspects were arrested during the searches, and that the 25-year-old was not found and was being sought. The 33-year-old was to be brought before a judge so that a warrant could be sought. The investigation was continuing.

The page that preserves this release is a law firm's blog, and the lawyer added a warning of his own: whether the police account was accurate was for a court to decide, not for a press spokesman, and the presumption of innocence applied to bikers as to anyone. The sources here do not report how the case ended.

In late August 2009 the interior ministry of Brandenburg banned Chicanos MC Barnim, a small group based in Eberswalde, near Berlin. Deutsche Welle reported that it had been founded in February that year and had 14 members. Police in Frankfurt (Oder) searched members' flats and the clubhouse, and the authorities also banned the group's website.

The interior minister, Jörg Schönbohm, called the ban "a clear signal that we will counter this gang trouble with all means legally at our disposal", and said that the formation and expansion of criminal associations would not be tolerated. Local media reported that hardly any members owned a motorcycle. What the police found, according to Deutsche Welle, were samurai swords, cudgels, brass knuckles and pistols, which Deutsche Welle said were used to exert influence in the doorman and drug scene of the region.

The ban came as the Bandidos and Hells Angels were fighting in Berlin and Brandenburg. Deutsche Welle noted a series of attacks and shootings in the previous weeks and the killing, earlier that month, of a Berlin gang member who had left the Hells Angels for the Bandidos. Schönbohm also pressed for a national ban on clubs like the Hells Angels and the Bandidos, though the federal interior minister could act only if the states concerned made a joint request.

In May 2010 the war was still on. On a night in late May, Berlin police checked four Hells Angels on the Sonnenallee in Neukölln and found a machete, a baseball bat and other weapons for striking and stabbing, the Berliner Zeitung reported. Police learned that the men meant to meet members of the Chicanos MC, whom the paper described as a supporter club of the Bandidos. Plain-clothes officers had seen the Chicanos in the same street, and armed police made them leave.

The Hells Angels rode off, met eleven more of their members and came back, and the Chicanos reappeared. Police stepped in before the two sides came to blows; it was said afterwards that the officers' service weapons persuaded the bikers not to fight. About 15 Hells Angels were then investigated on suspicion of forming an armed group.

The paper quoted Berlin's police president, Dieter Glietsch, telling the state parliament the week before that there was no sign of a truce: "Der Rockerkrieg ist noch voll im Gang", in his words, that the biker war was still in full swing. It gave among the causes the switch of 70 Bandidos to the Hells Angels in February 2010 and the killing, the previous August, of a Hells Angels member it identified as Michael B. (Deutsche Welle, in 2009, described a murdered Berlin man as someone who had left the Hells Angels for the Bandidos.) The paper put the number of Berlin clubs backing the Hells Angels or their rivals at 17, with 800 members, and said the Bandidos operated in the north of the city and the Hells Angels in the south.

The best-documented court case comes from Sweden. In early 2013 the Göteborgs-Tidningen revealed that an unofficial Bandidos sub-group called Chicanos Trestad, named for the three-town area of Trollhättan, Vänersborg and Uddevalla, was trying to establish itself. Police told the paper they noticed the group at the turn of the year and had watched it carry out a kind of extortion called "bötning", fining people for supposed debts. Their headquarters was an industrial unit in Vänersborg, which police described as an illegal after-hours club; it closed after the police operation.

In early February 2013 four members were arrested and remanded. At trial they faced two extortion charges. The first dated from late 2012 in Mellerud. According to the prosecution, two men in their mid-twenties demanded 5,000 kronor from a man of the same age, claiming he had sold drugs on the club's turf, and then demanded another 5,000. The man had to borrow the first sum from his mother. The second charge concerned a 22-year-old in Uddevalla, who was allegedly told to pay 5,000 kronor and hand over his puppy, which two of the four fetched from his girlfriend's home. The charges also covered theft, handling stolen goods and drug offences found during searches.

The paper reported that fear of the group meant only two complainants dared to appear in court; Magnusson called the two cases the tip of an iceberg, though he had no figure. The paper reported that the man named as president, 25, had told police that supporting the Bandidos was like cheering for a hockey team, and had admitted at trial that he was a Chicanos member. He was already serving 14 months for an earlier extortion committed, according to the appeal court's judgment, in the colours of No Surrender, a now-dissolved Bandidos sub-group.

The paper reported that the group had also tried to recruit from Black Cobra, and that a brawl between the two had brought police to Strandgatan in Trollhättan the previous week. About ten people were there, three in club jackets, but police saw no assault and took no further action. Police said the quarrel was about drug sales and market share.

By December 2013 the paper reported that the former president, then 26, had been sentenced to one and a half years in prison for assault, extortion, theft and drug offences and was to be released on parole. Two other leading figures had also been sentenced, the paper said, and, according to information given to the paper, the police feared that his return could set off a power struggle inside the group. Magnusson said police would handle any rise in activity.
content.h2: Norway, Sandviken and the German badge ban
content.p: In April 2014 the Fædrelandsvennen reported that a Chicanos club had been set up in Kristiansand, southern Norway, apparently tied to the same clubhouse as a Bandidos probationary chapter. Leif Vagle, who leads police work on organised crime in the Agder region, said the Chicanos had five to ten men aged 20 to 30, roughly the same number as the Bandidos there, and that police were unsure whether they were an equal partner or a crew working for the Bandidos. He added that Swedish media had written during the past year about Chicanos in western Sweden extorting people.

In Sandviken, Sweden, Arbetarbladet reported in October 2015 that a 23-year-old named as president of the local Chicanos was convicted of minor drug offences, doping offences, unlicensed driving and drunk driving, and given day-fines. The paper said senior Bandidos had visited the clubhouse that weekend and that police ran an extra traffic check nearby.

In Germany the symbols themselves became illegal. From Thursday 16 March 2017 a nationwide ban took effect on displaying the badges of eight groups, among them the Hells Angels, Bandidos and Chicanos MC. North Rhine-Westphalia's interior minister, Ralf Jäger, said the emblems expressed this criminal scene's contempt for the state. The ministry said 48 chapters in the state were affected, with about 1,500 members in all, and that the ban applied whatever the local name beneath the emblem. Anyone who defied it would lose the jacket and face a criminal complaint.

Later court records also mention the club in passing. A Swedish court judgment from October 2017, reported by Expressen, convicted three Norwegians of a serious sexual assault in Värmland that began as an attempt to extort money from the victim, giving the men four years each and the woman two. One of them told the court he was a member of Chicanos MC in Norway, a sub-group of the Bandidos. A probation report in the case said the Bandidos are considered to meet the European Union's definition of organised crime. The three denied the sexual assault but admitted assault to some degree.
